guide.title: The Sick Rose — a guided reading and memorisation plan
guide.description: An unhurried reading of William Blake’s poem, with short passages, images, sound and gentle returns to the text.

metadata.chunkingStrategy: Passages within original stanzas; chunks of at most two lines. Read aloud and recall at your own pace, without scored exercises.

poem.title: The Sick Rose
poem.author: William Blake
poem.text:
O Rose, thou art sick!
The invisible worm
That flies in the night,
In the howling storm,

Has found out thy bed
Of crimson joy:
And his dark secret love
Does thy life destroy.

metadata.edition: University of Toronto Representative Poetry Online, citing Songs of Experience (1794), Blake’s Illuminated Books, ed. David Bindman. Two four-line stanzas. RPO punctuation differs from the Poetry Foundation transcription; follow RPO throughout.

coverImage.alt: Watercolour painting of a drooping crimson rose with a small worm beneath its curved stem against a dark blue-grey background.

sessions.title: An unseen arrival
sessions.focusSummary: Hold the rose, the invisible worm and the storm together.

pages.title: An invitation to read
pages.bodyMarkdown: Blake addresses a rose as though it could hear him. The eight lines offer a few vivid things and an unsettling relationship between them. Begin by speaking the whole poem without trying to solve it. Its images can stay open while the words become familiar. Thou means you; thy means your.

pages.title: The whole poem
pages.bodyMarkdown:
O Rose, thou art sick!
The invisible worm
That flies in the night,
In the howling storm,

Has found out thy bed
Of crimson joy:
And his dark secret love
Does thy life destroy.

pages.title: Stay with these lines
pages.bodyMarkdown: Read the passage aloud, following the sentence through the line endings. Pause over an image or sound that draws your attention.

pages.title: An unseen arrival
pages.bodyMarkdown: The opening is an urgent address. After it, the sentence begins following a worm that cannot be seen and yet flies. Rather than making the scene tidier, let those details retain their strangeness. Night and storm give us a setting without explaining the danger. The stanza ends with a comma in this edition: the sentence will continue across the gap. Keep the pause without making it a full stop.

pages.title: Let the words return
pages.bodyMarkdown: Hold the scene in mind and look away from the words. Try saying one or two lines, then return to the text wherever you need it. Join the passage together at a comfortable pace.

pages.title: A moment to linger
pages.prompt: What do you picture when the poem describes something as invisible?

pages.title: A place to pause
pages.bodyMarkdown: You can leave the passage here for a while. If an image or a sound stays with you, let it. Return whenever you would like to hear how the next lines continue the thought.

sessions.title: Crimson joy
sessions.focusSummary: Follow the unfinished sentence into its disturbing conclusion.

pages.title: Return to the previous passage
pages.bodyMarkdown: Read these lines aloud once. If you like, look away and let their scene bring back a phrase before looking again. There is no need to hurry.

pages.title: Stay with these lines
pages.bodyMarkdown: Read the passage aloud, following the sentence through the line endings. Pause over an image or sound that draws your attention.

pages.title: Crimson joy
pages.bodyMarkdown: The first line completes the action begun in the previous stanza. Bed might belong to a garden or to an intimate human space; crimson offers colour without settling the association. Notice how love is placed beside secrecy and destruction. You can explore disease, desire or harm as possibilities, keeping each close to the actual words. Read both stanzas aloud and hear how little explanation the poem supplies.

pages.title: Let the words return
pages.bodyMarkdown: Hold the scene in mind and look away from the words. Try saying one or two lines, then return to the text wherever you need it. Join the passage together at a comfortable pace.

pages.title: A moment to linger
pages.prompt: Which word most unsettles your first impression of the rose, and why?

pages.title: Read from the beginning
pages.bodyMarkdown:
O Rose, thou art sick!
The invisible worm
That flies in the night,
In the howling storm,

Has found out thy bed
Of crimson joy:
And his dark secret love
Does thy life destroy.

pages.title: Keep the poem near
pages.bodyMarkdown: Let the poem rest for now. A phrase may return later, or you may want to read it aloud again with a different emphasis. Familiarity can grow through small, unhurried returns.
